strengths: Clear and relevant problem formulation: The paper tackles a well-defined and practically important limitation in existing location-scale noise model (LSNM) causal discovery methods, which predominantly assume symmetric noise distributions and fail under skewness.

Technically sound estimation pipeline: The authors develop a well-structured optimization procedure combining Bayesian optimization for penalty parameters, CMA-ES for global exploration, and a custom Expectation Conditional Maximization (ECM) algorithm adapted to heteroscedastic generalized additive models (GAMs) under skew-normal likelihoods.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The experimental suite is thorough, covering both controlled skew-noise benchmarks (including misspecified generalized normal noise) and 13 established bivariate benchmark datasets, alongside multivariate experiments on synthetic DAGs.

Practical multivariate formulation: Proposition 5.1 provides a clean and useful efficiency shortcut, proving that DAG scoring within a Markov equivalence class (MEC) can be restricted to nodes with incident unoriented edges.

Insightful ablation and diagnostics: The paper includes meaningful ablations demonstrating the necessity of the ECM refinement over pure heuristic search and examining the trade-offs between Gaussian and KDE-based marginal likelihood estimation.
weaknesses: High computational burden and limited scalability: The combination of Bayesian optimization, multi-start CMA-ES, and multi-iteration ECM makes parameter estimation demanding. While viable for bivariate tasks and small graphs (d <= 10), SKEWD-MV will struggle to scale to larger or denser DAGs where the number of parent-child configurations grows rapidly.

Heavy reliance on initial constraint-based MEC estimation: In the multivariate setting, SKEWD-MV relies on the PC algorithm to output an accurate MEC. Any conditional independence errors made by PC in the presence of complex non-linear heteroscedastic noise directly propagate to the final graph estimate.

Modest theoretical novelty: The identifiability of LSNMs is established by leveraging existing general results (Immer et al., 2023; Strobl & Lasko, 2023). The primary contribution is methodological and algorithmic rather than foundational identifiability theory.

Discussion of baseline anomalies: In Table 5, IGCI-G achieves nearly 100% accuracy on the skewed benchmark pairs despite being developed for deterministic/low-noise mechanisms. A deeper analytical discussion of why this strongly misspecified baseline performs so well would enhance the experimental analysis.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant limitation in existing location-scale noise models (LSNMs), namely the vulnerability of symmetric/Gaussian noise assumptions to skewed error distributions, which often causes spurious dependence in residuals and misidentifies causal direction.

Derives a coherent estimation framework for skew-normal LSNMs combining B-spline GAMs with a penalized log-likelihood, solved via a structured optimization pipeline (Bayesian optimization for smoothing penalties, CMA-ES initialization, and ECM refinement).

Provides extensive empirical validation across 6 newly designed skewed datasets as well as 13 established benchmarks (e.g., Tübingen, SIM, Net, Multi), demonstrating robust bivariate cause-effect inference even when true noise distributions exceed the theoretical skewness/kurtosis bounds of the skew-normal family.

Includes useful ablations and extensions, such as demonstrating the necessity of the ECM refinement over pure heuristic search, exploring non-parametric KDE for marginal distributions, and formalizing the score-based multivariate extension over Markov equivalence classes (Proposition 5.1).
weaknesses: High computational complexity and limited multivariate scalability: The estimation procedure requires Bayesian optimization, multi-start CMA-ES, and iterative ECM for every candidate conditional. In the multivariate setting (SKEWD-MV), candidate parent-child configurations grow exponentially with the degree of undirected edges in the MEC, restricting practical applicability to small graphs ($d \le 10$).

Methodological novelty is largely an integration of existing techniques: The identifiability relies on existing theorems (Immer et al., 2023; Strobl & Lasko, 2023), the ECM updates closely adapt the formulation of Ferreira et al. (2023) to GAMs, and the multivariate search relies on standard PC-based MEC initialization.

Sensitivity to marginal distributional assumptions in SKEWD-LL: The default likelihood-scoring variant assumes standard Gaussian marginals after standardization. As demonstrated in Appendix B.6, when true marginal distributions deviate significantly from Gaussianity (e.g., in Tübingen and SIM benchmarks), this assumption degrades performance unless nonparametric density estimation is used, which itself introduces variance.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and realistic limitation in existing location-scale noise model (LSNM) causal discovery algorithms, which predominantly assume symmetric noise distributions and fail under skewness.

The proposed estimation strategy is sound and carefully designed, combining generalized additive models (GAMs) with roughness penalties, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES heuristic search, and an ECM algorithm derived from the latent-variable representation of the skew-normal distribution.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering novel synthetic benchmarks with varied skewness levels (including out-of-distribution generalized normal noise), 13 established benchmarks (such as the Tübingen pairs), and multivariate DAG recovery experiments.

The paper is very well-written and clear. Helpful visualizations (Figures 1 and 3) effectively demonstrate how symmetric noise assumptions induce spurious dependence in residuals and why skew-normal modeling resolves this issue.

Ablation studies thoroughly substantiate the algorithmic design choices, notably proving the necessity of the ECM refinement over pure CMA-ES and analyzing parametric vs. nonparametric (KDE) marginal density estimation.
weaknesses: The core theoretical identifiability results rely entirely on prior work (Immer et al., 2023; Strobl & Lasko, 2023); the primary methodological novelty lies in fitting skew-normal GAMs and applying them within standard causal discovery frameworks.

The computational pipeline (Bayesian optimization + CMA-ES + ECM iterations per candidate model) is computationally demanding, restricting the multivariate extension to small, sparse graphs (evaluated up to d = 10) where the Markov equivalence class contains manageable parent-child configurations.

The bivariate likelihood-scoring variant (SKEWD-LL) discards marginal log-likelihoods by assuming standardized variables are Gaussian; as shown in Appendix B.6, this hurts performance when marginals deviate strongly from Gaussianity (e.g., on the Tübingen benchmark).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation in causal discovery within location-scale noise models (LSNMs), where prevailing methods assume symmetric (Gaussian or Student-t) noise distributions that degrade under skewness.

Technically sound optimization framework that adapts penalized B-spline regression with an Expectation Conditional Maximization (ECM) algorithm specifically tailored for skew-normal heteroscedastic models, initialized robustly via CMA-ES and Bayesian optimization.

Comprehensive empirical study covering both newly constructed skewed noise benchmarks (with skewness up to 1.750) and 13 established causal discovery benchmarks, demonstrating clear advantages on skewed heteroscedastic data.
Helpful ablation study demonstrating that the ECM refinement provides substantial accuracy gains over heuristic CMA-ES optimization alone.
weaknesses: High computational overhead: Running Bayesian optimization with 8-fold cross-validation, followed by CMA-ES (population size 100, up to 5000 iterations) and an ECM refinement (up to 5000 iterations) per directed edge is computationally intensive; the paper lacks explicit wall-clock runtime comparisons against baselines.

The likelihood scoring variant (SKEWD-LL) assumes that the marginal distribution of the cause is standard normal after standardization, an assumption that frequently fails in real-world data and causes notable performance drops on certain benchmark suites (e.g., Tübingen, SIM).
Restricted strictly to the bivariate setting, without theoretical or algorithmic extensions to multivariate directed acyclic graphs.

On existing standard benchmarks (Table 1), SKEWD-IT and SKEWD-LL are outperformed by existing methods such as ROCHE, and the strikingly high performance of IGCI-G on the synthetic skewed datasets is not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically relevant limitation in existing location-scale noise model (LSNM) causal discovery methods, which overwhelmingly assume symmetric (Gaussian or Student's t) error distributions.

The proposed method, SKEWD, is technically sound: it formulates a penalized spline-based heteroscedastic skew-normal regression model and devises an effective multi-stage optimization pipeline combining Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES heuristic search, and an Expectation Conditional Maximization (ECM) refinement.

The paper provides a thorough empirical evaluation featuring newly constructed skewed benchmarks (using both skew-normal and generalized normal distributions) alongside 13 standard causal discovery benchmarks, demonstrating notable robustness against severe skewness compared to baselines like LOCI and QCCD.

The manuscript includes insightful ablations and graphical diagnostic plots (Figures 1 and 3) that clearly illustrate why standard Gaussian/symmetric models fail under skewness and how SKEWD corrects residual dependence.
weaknesses: High computational overhead: The estimation procedure requires an 8-fold cross-validated Bayesian optimization step, CMA-ES with population size 100 for up to 5,000 iterations, and a subsequent ECM refinement up to 5,000 iterations, run in both causal directions. The paper lacks an empirical runtime analysis and wall-clock comparisons against baselines.

Theoretical simplification in likelihood scoring: For SKEWD-LL, dropping the marginal log-likelihoods relies on assuming standard Gaussian marginal distributions after standardization (Section 4 and Appendix A). In datasets where the cause itself is heavily skewed or non-Gaussian, this assumption is violated and may introduce scoring biases.

Performance on established benchmarks is mixed: On the 13 established benchmarks (Table 1), ROCHE achieves higher overall accuracy (87.69% vs. 85.02% for SKEWD-IT and 77.43% for SKEWD-LL) and AUDRC. Additionally, the heuristic baseline IGCI-G achieves near-perfect performance on the synthetic skewed benchmarks despite misspecification, which warrants deeper discussion.
The scope is strictly limited to bivariate causal discovery; no extension or discussion of topological ordering in multivariate DAGs is provided.

strengths: Clear motivation: Addressing skewed noise in location-scale noise models (LSNMs) targets a realistic and known failure mode of existing Gaussian-based causal discovery methods.

Principled modeling: Incorporating the skew-normal distribution with B-spline parameterization for both location and scale functions provides an elegant parametric generalization of standard Gaussian LSNMs.

Comprehensive synthetic suite: The introduction of skewed benchmarks (ANs and LSs with skew-normal and generalized normal noise) systematically investigates performance across controlled degrees of skewness.
Ablation study: The appendix provides a helpful ablation demonstrating the necessity of the Expectation Conditional Maximization (ECM) refinement step over the initial CMA-ES heuristic.
weaknesses: Dubious theoretical justification for likelihood scoring: The argument in Section 4 and Appendix A for neglecting the marginal likelihoods relies on standardizing the variables and treating them as standard normal. Because empirical standardization forces the sum of squares to $n-1$, the evaluated standard normal log-likelihoods are identical by construction, regardless of the true marginal distributions. In settings where variables are heavily skewed or non-Gaussian (the core motivation of the paper), the true marginal densities $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ will not be standard normal, leading to substantial likelihood misspecification.

Underwhelming real-world and general benchmark performance: On the 13 established benchmarks (Table 1), SKEWD-LL (77.43%) and SKEWD-IT (85.02%) lag behind ROCHE (87.69%). On the real-world Tübingen benchmark (Table 6), SKEWD-LL achieves only 45.97% (worse than random guessing) and SKEWD-IT achieves 66.57%, noticeably behind ROCHE (77.27%) and GRCI (81.59%).

Heavy computational pipeline without runtime benchmarks: The proposed parameter estimation combines Bayesian optimization (60 candidate evaluations with 8-fold CV), stochastic CMA-ES search with population 100 up to 5000 iterations, and ECM up to 5000 iterations for each bivariate direction. No runtime analysis, wall-clock measurements, or scaling considerations are reported.

Limited novelty on identifiability: The paper relies directly on existing identifiability results for general LSNMs from Immer et al. (2023) and Strobl & Lasko (2023) without providing new theoretical characterizations specific to the skew-normal setting.
